name: LL-37

lead: LL-37 is a natural antimicrobial peptide made by skin and immune cells, and the only cathelicidin humans make. Forum posters discuss it for clearing acne, healing skin and anti-aging, drawing on its role in fighting skin bacteria and calming inflammation.

It damages microbial membranes and attracts immune cells through the FPRL1 receptor, and vitamin D raises its production. Published research is mainly on its natural role in skin infection and in atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and rosacea. The few registered LL-37 trials involve melanoma and diabetic foot ulcers; no trial for acne or cosmetic skin improvement was found.

paras: It is discussed in appearance communities as a research peptide for acne or skin quality. It is investigational, with no standard routine or established timeline.
It is investigational and not an approved drug. Excess LL-37 is suspected in rosacea and psoriasis inflammation. No safety data for cosmetic use were found.

forums.title: LL-37 Has anyone tried it for acne?

angle.text: LL-37 is the body's own antimicrobial skin peptide, and forum posters discuss it for clearing acne, healing skin and anti-aging by lowering acne bacteria and inflammation. These uses draw on its immune biology; research covers skin infection and inflammatory skin disease.

lead: LL-37 is a 37-amino-acid antimicrobial peptide and the only cathelicidin made by humans. It is cleaved from a precursor protein, hCAP18, and is produced by neutrophils and epithelial cells including skin keratinocytes [1][2]. It is part of the innate immune system and also signals to immune cells [1].

In appearance communities it is sometimes discussed as a research peptide for acne or skin quality. Published work is predominantly on its natural role in skin infection and inflammatory skin disease, including atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and rosacea, rather than on LL-37 as a cosmetic treatment [3][4]. No clinical trial of LL-37 for acne or cosmetic skin improvement was found.

paras: LL-37 is released from hCAP18 by proteolytic cleavage and acts on microbial membranes. It is chemotactic for neutrophils, monocytes and T cells through the receptor FPRL1 [1]. A mouse study found that a cathelicidin protects skin from invasive bacterial infection [2].

Vitamin D raises cathelicidin expression. Skin from people with atopic dermatitis was found to have lower LL-37 levels than psoriatic skin, linked to a higher susceptibility to skin infections [3]. Excess processed LL-37 is also suspected of contributing to rosacea and, bound to self nucleic acids, of sustaining inflammation in psoriasis. These roles are described in the Wikipedia article on cathelicidin.

Registered trials involving LL-37 are few and mostly observational or biomarker-based. A small phase 1/2 trial examined intratumoral LL-37 in melanoma (4 participants) [5]. A phase 2 trial of an LL-37 cream for diabetic foot ulcers (40 participants) is registered with unknown status [6]. Other registered studies measure endogenous LL-37 levels in periodontal and peri-implant disease and in smoking exposure [7][8]. None addresses acne, scarring or cosmetic skin outcomes.

Wikipedia notes that barriers to therapeutic use include rapid breakdown by proteases, limited bioavailability, production cost and restriction to injected or infused routes, and that modified analogues such as SAAP-148 are under study.

lore.intro: Discussion on looksmax.org is sparse; one thread asks whether LL-37 helps acne [9].
